content: The Guidelines for Surveillance of Drug Resistance in Tuberculosis, 5th Edition is a comprehensive document published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2015. It provides detailed recommendations for monitoring and addressing drug resistance in tuberculosis (TB). 1. Purpose and Scope: The guidelines aim to assist national tuberculosis control programs (NTPs) in developing robust surveillance mechanisms to monitor drug resistance in TB. The ultimate goal is to establish routine, continuous surveillance systems based on systematic drug susceptibility testing (DST). These systems are critical for understanding the burden and distribution of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). 2. Historical Context: This is the fifth edition of the guidelines, building on previous editions published in 1994, 1997, 2003, and 2009. It incorporates advancements in laboratory diagnostics, such as molecular line probe assays and the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, which allow for rapid detection of drug resistance. The guidelines also reflect 20 years of experience from the Global Project on Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Resistance Surveillance, initiated by WHO and the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease. 3. Global Project on Anti-TB Drug Resistance Surveillance: Since its inception in 1994, the Global Project has systematically collected and analyzed data on drug resistance from 144 countries, representing 95% of the global population. This project has provided critical insights into the global burden of MDR-TB and XDR-TB, helping countries plan and scale up management strategies. 4. Surveillance Approaches: Two main approaches to drug resistance surveillance are outlined: Continuous Surveillance: Based on routine DST of all TB patients, this approach provides ongoing data on drug resistance patterns and trends. It is most effective in high-income countries with well-established laboratory systems. Periodic Surveys: In resource-limited settings where routine DST is not feasible, periodic surveys of randomly selected TB patients are recommended. These surveys provide representative data on drug resistance and can detect trends over time. 5. Integration of Molecular Technologies: The guidelines recommend incorporating molecular technologies, such as WHO-endorsed rapid diagnostic tests, into surveillance systems. These technologies can be used alone or as a screening tool before culture-based methods. The choice of diagnostic algorithm depends on the survey's objectives and available resources. 6. Monitoring Trends in Drug Resistance: For countries with recent, high-quality survey data but limited capacity for routine DST, the guidelines suggest using rapid molecular technologies at sentinel sites to monitor trends in drug resistance over time. 7. Standardization and Comparability: The guidelines emphasize the importance of standardized criteria for surveillance to ensure comparability of results across countries and over time. This includes consistent patient classifications, quality-assured laboratory processes, and comprehensive data recording and reporting. 8. Target Audience: The primary audience for these guidelines includes NTPs, particularly coordination teams composed of NTP managers, laboratory specialists, epidemiologists, statisticians, and logistics experts. 9. Key Updates from Previous Editions: Incorporation of molecular technologies into surveys. Recommendations for monitoring trends using rapid molecular technologies in sentinel sites. Emphasis on the need for sustainable surveillance systems tailored to country-specific capacities and needs. 10. Challenges and Recommendations: While continuous surveillance systems are ideal, many countries lack the capacity to implement them. In such cases, periodic surveys remain the foundation of drug resistance surveillance. Countries are encouraged to take a long-term view of surveillance, designing systems that are sustainable and capable of evaluating trends over time. 11. Global Impact: The guidelines highlight the critical role of surveillance data in quantifying the global burden of MDR-TB and XDR-TB, guiding public health responses, and supporting the scale-up of TB management programs. 12. Call to Action: WHO urges all member states to achieve universal access to diagnosis and treatment of MDR-TB and XDR-TB. Strengthening health information and surveillance systems is essential for detecting and monitoring the epidemiological profile of drug-resistant TB and evaluating progress in its prevention and control. These guidelines serve as a vital resource for public health professionals, policymakers, and researchers working to combat the global threat of drug-resistant TB.
